title: Together
full_review:
A young violin prodigy and his father travel from a rural Chinese town to big-city Beijing in search of a music teacher in the emotionally telling "Together" (United Artists).Weaving arger cultural issues into a father-son dynamic, director Chen Kaige hits all the right notes in composing a modest yet eloquent coming-of-age symphony.

Xiaochun (Tang Yun), a gifted musician, lives in a backwater town with his father, Liu Cheng (Liu Peiqi), a simple but well-intentioned cook. Realizing that his son's talent, if it is to bloom, needs something richer than provincial soil, Cheng takes his meager savings and heads off with Xiaochun to Beijing, a metropolis brimming with opportunities and reputable violin instructors.

Once in Beijing, Cheng's hope of enrolling Xiaochun in an top-notch conservatory are quickly dashed, as he gets a crash course in the politics of privilege, learning that wealth and pedigree are prerequisites over talent. Undeterred, Cheng's homespun tenacity wins out, prompting him to secure Professor Jiang (Wang Ziwen), a cultured but cantankerous virtuoso, as a tutor for his son. Though demanding, Jiang is less concerned with money than with instilling in Xiaochun a passion for music -- an attitude which resonates with his sensitive pupil.

However, Xiaochun's progress is thrown a curve when his father petitions Professor Yu (Chen Kaige), Beijing's premier "star-maker," to consider Xiaochun as his protege. Yu, recognizing the boy's potential, takes him under his wing. But Xiaochun quickly sees through the autocratic maestro's guise of altruism, and is left to choose between remaining true to himself and disappointing the one person who matters most: his father.

On the surface, this film is an uplifting story about the love shared between a father and his son, a gracefully crafted melody of tears and laughter. The filmmaker displays a genuine regard for the self-sacrifice and simple peasant heroism embodied in Cheng, whose unadorned devotion to his son is the narrative's emotional engine, fueling it with humanity and poetry -- made more poignant by a revelation near the film's conclusion.

Yet percolating underneath the father-son plot is a more nuanced cultural subtext represented by the two instructors. The filmmaker juxtaposes the characters, creating dialectic between tradition and modernity, between art and commerce, between the soul of China's cultural inheritance and the consumerism that is threatening that patrimony. Contrasting Jiang's modest lifestyle is the more ambitious Yu, surrounded by westernized opulence, symbolizing a dark side of capitalism stoked by greed.

Inspired by experiences growing up during China's Cultural Revolution, director Kaige observes, "People everywhere in China are becoming more defined by material things and status. The fear of being censored by the government under the old regime is being replaced with the fear of being poor. It is verging on a spiritual crisis in Chinese society."

Chen Hong, who plays Lili, a goodhearted neighbor with whom Xiaochun is smitten, supplies a much needed feminine, nurturing element to an otherwise all-male equation. She also provides a subplot which offers some of the film's most tender moments.

Subtitles.

Due to emotionally complex relationships, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.
